# MIPS64 big endian: the same snippets as mips-programs.txt, plus a few
# doubleword ones. See that file for why every snippet ends with `.p2align 6`.
#
# `$t0`-`$t7` are spelled numerically here for the ABI reason explained at the
# top of mips64.txt, and `la` of a symbol is left out because N64 llvm-mc
# expands it into a six-instruction 64-bit address.

=== ddiv loop
loop:
ld $4, 0($5)
daddiu $5, $5, 8
dsubu $6, $6, $7
bnez $6, loop
.p2align 6

=== bgez with doubleword work in the loop
loop:
dsll $4, $4, 1
dsrl32 $5, $5, 3
bgez $4, loop
.p2align 6

=== beq backward
foo:
beq $1, $2, foo
.p2align 6

=== beq across two instructions
foo:
addiu $4, $4, 1
addiu $5, $5, -1
beq $4, $5, foo
.p2align 6

=== bne
foo:
bne $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== blez
foo:
blez $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgtz
foo:
bgtz $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bltz
foo:
bltz $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgez
foo:
bgez $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bltzal
foo:
bltzal $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgezal
foo:
bgezal $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== b
foo:
b foo
.p2align 6

=== bal
foo:
bal foo
.p2align 6

=== beqz
foo:
beqz $v0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bnez
foo:
bnez $v0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bge
foo:
bge $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgt
foo:
bgt $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== ble
foo:
ble $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== blt
foo:
blt $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgeu
foo:
bgeu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgtu
foo:
bgtu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bleu
foo:
bleu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bltu
foo:
bltu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bge against zero folds to bgez
foo:
bge $a0, $zero, foo
.p2align 6

=== blt against zero folds to bltz
foo:
blt $a0, $zero, foo
.p2align 6

=== jr
foo:
jr $ra
.p2align 6

=== jalr one operand links through ra
foo:
jalr $25
.p2align 6

=== jalr two operands
foo:
jalr $s0, $25
.p2align 6

=== bc1f
foo:
bc1f foo
.p2align 6

=== bc1t
foo:
bc1t foo
.p2align 6

=== a backwards loop
loop:
lw $8, 0($a0)
addiu $a0, $a0, 4
addiu $a1, $a1, -1
sw $8, 0($a1)
bnez $a1, loop
.p2align 6

# A forward branch would normally be thrown off by llvm-mc's inserted delay
# slot, since the extra word sits between the branch and its target. Aligning
# the target absorbs that word too, so the measured distance stays the same.
=== beq forward over an alignment
beq $1, $2, end
.p2align 6
end:
nop

=== bnez forward over an alignment
bnez $a0, end
.p2align 6
end:
nop

=== j
foo:
j foo
.p2align 6

=== jal
foo:
jal foo
.p2align 6

# Unresolved references leave their field zero and emit a relocation, so the
# .text bytes are comparable even though the addresses are not yet known.
=== explicit hi and lo halves
lui $a0, %hi(extern_sym)
addiu $a0, $a0, %lo(extern_sym)
lw $a1, %lo(extern_sym)($a0)
nop

=== hi and lo of a local symbol
sym = 0x12345678
lui $a0, %hi(sym)
addiu $a0, $a0, %lo(sym)
nop

=== hi and lo where the low half is negative
sym = 0x1234abcd
lui $a0, %hi(sym)
addiu $a0, $a0, %lo(sym)
nop

# `j` takes an absolute address, so a number means the same thing to both
# assemblers here (unlike a conditional branch, where llvm-mc reads a bare
# number as the displacement). The top four bits come from the PC, so a target
# above 256 MB is not out of range.
=== j to an absolute address
j 0x400000
.p2align 6

=== jal into kseg0
jal 0x80001000
.p2align 6

=== j to the last word of a region
j 0x0ffffffc
.p2align 6
